In what year was Saddam Hussein born?
Saddam Hussein: The policies and ideologies he championed are collectively known as Saddamism, a right-wing variant of Ba'athism.
In what year was Jerry Springer born?
Jerry Springer: Gerald Norman Springer (February 13, 1944 – April 27, 2023) was a British-American broadcaster, television host, journalist, actor, lawyer, and politician.
In what year was Mustafa Kemal Atatürk born?
Mustafa Kemal Atatürk: Atatürk denounced CUP leadership for encouraging a politicised military –and was subsequently sidelined– as they established a new authoritarian regime.
In what year was Simón Bolívar born?
Simón Bolívar: Bolívar was born in Caracas in the Captaincy General of Venezuela into a wealthy family of American-born Spaniards (criollo) but lost both parents as a child.
In what year did Pablo Escobar die?
Pablo Escobar: In the 1982 Colombian parliamentary election, Escobar was elected as an alternate member of the Chamber of Representatives as part of the Liberal Party.
In what year did Sam Manekshaw die?
Sam Manekshaw: Manekshaw joined the first intake of the Indian Military Academy at Dehradun in 1932.
In what year was Wessex founded?
Wessex: The Kingdom of the West Saxons, also known as the Kingdom of Wessex, was an Anglo-Saxon kingdom in the south of Great Britain, from around 519 until around 927.
In what year was Polish People's Republic founded?
Polish People's Republic: It was also where the Warsaw Pact was founded.
In what year was Scuderia AlphaTauri founded?
Scuderia AlphaTauri S.p.A., commonly known as AlphaTauri, was an Italian Formula One racing team and constructor that competed from 2020 to 2023.
Champaran Satyagraha: Mahatma Gandhi. It was a farmer's uprising that took place in Champaran district of Bihar in the Indian subcontinent, during the British colonial period.
Spanish Empire: Catholic Monarchs. The Spanish Empire, sometimes referred to as the Hispanic Monarchy or the Catholic Monarchy, was a colonial empire that existed between 1492 and 1976.
In which country was Kuru kingdom?
Kuru kingdom: India. The Kuru Kingdom was a Vedic Indo-Aryan tribal union in northern India of the Bharata and Puru tribes.
In which country did the Second Battle of Fallujah take place?
Second Battle of Fallujah: Iraq. After that battle, control of the city was transferred to an Iraqi-run local security force, which began stockpiling weapons and building complex defenses.
In which country did the Battle of Ramillies take place?
Battle of Ramillies: Spanish Netherlands. The Battle of Ramillies, fought on 23 May 1706, was a battle of the War of the Spanish Succession.
In which country is Khmer Rouge based?
Khmer Rouge: Cambodia. Although it originally fought against Sihanouk, the Khmer Rouge changed its position and supported Sihanouk following the CCP's advice.
Magadha: India. Magadha (IPA: [məɡəd̪ʰaː]) was a region and kingdom in ancient India, based in the eastern Ganges Plain.
In which country is Bambatha Rebellion?
Bambatha Rebellion: South Africa. It was sparked by unpopular taxation policies levied by the Natal colonial administration, which exacerbated ongoing economic crises.
In which country was Heaven's Gate?
Heaven's Gate (religious group): United States. Heaven's Gate was an American new religious movement known primarily for the mass suicide of its members in 1997.
In which country was Seoul Spring?
Seoul Spring: South Korea. The Seoul Spring (Korean: 서울의 봄) was a period of democratization in South Korea from 26 October 1979 to 17 May 1980.
In which country is Orange Revolution?
Orange Revolution: Ukraine. The nationwide protests succeeded when the results of the original runoff were annulled, and a re-vote was ordered by Ukraine's Supreme Court for 26 December 2004.

Which of these was an official language of the Kingdom of Greece?
Kingdom of Greece: Katharevousa. The country remained a kingdom until 1924, when the Second Hellenic Republic was proclaimed.
Which of these was an official language of Democratic Republic of Afghanistan?
Democratic Republic of Afghanistan: Pashto. The Democratic Republic of Afghanistan, later known as the Republic of Afghanistan, was the left-wing led Afghan state from 1978 to 1992.
Of which country was Hanseongbu the capital?
Hanseongbu is the capital of Joseon. It was founded by Taejo of Joseon in 1392 and replaced by the Korean Empire in 1897.
An SS officer tasked by Reinhard Heydrich with managing the rail logistics of mass deportations after the 1942 Wannsee Conference, this Holocaust organizer was captured and tried — who was he?

Adolf Eichmann (German; 19 March 1906 - 1 June 1962) was a German-Austrian official of the Nazi Party, an officer of the Schutzstaffel (SS), a convicted war criminal, and one of the major organizers of the Holocaust.
Introduced to Hitler by Dietrich Eckart, this Baltic German edited the Völkischer Beobachter and ran the Nazi bureau for cultural policy and surveillance that bore his own name — who was he?
Alfred Rosenberg was Nazi theorist and war criminal (1893–1946).
He founded the antisemitic precursor to the Nazi Party and mentored a young Adolf Hitler, only to be pushed out as chairman in a 1921 power struggle — who is he?
Anton Drexler (13 June 1884 - 24 February 1942) was a German far-right political agitator for the Vlkisch movement in the 1920s.

She founded the New York chapter of the Daughters of Bilitis, edited its magazine The Ladder, and worked with Frank Kameny on early picket lines protesting the U.S. government's ban on employing gay people. Who was she?
Barbara Gittings (July 31, 1932 - February 18, 2007) was an American LGBTQ activist.
While starving himself in a Northern Ireland prison in 1981 to protest the loss of Special Category Status, this IRA man was actually elected to the UK Parliament — who was he?
Bobby Sands (9 March 1954 - 5 May 1981) was a member of the Provisional Irish Republican Army (IRA) who died on hunger strike while imprisoned at HM Prison Maze in Northern Ireland.

Fought between Bolivia and Paraguay from 1932 to 1935 over a petroleum-rich region beneath a semi-arid plain, this conflict was the first in South America to feature machine guns, armored vehicles, and airplanes — what's the war?
Chaco War was fought from 1932 to 1935. The Chaco War (Spanish: Guerra del Chaco, Guarani: Cháko Ñorairõ) was fought from 1932 to 1935.
The first African-American to represent New Jersey in the US Senate, a seat held since 2013, this politician previously served as mayor of Newark from 2006 to 2013 — who is he?
Cory Booker (born April 27, 1969) is an American politician and lawyer serving as a United States senator from New Jersey, a seat he has held since 2013.

The granddaughter of the last ruling Maharaja of the princely state of Jaipur, this Bharatiya Janata Party politician has served as Deputy Chief Minister of Rajasthan since December 2023 — who is she?

Diya Kumari (born 30 January 1971) is an Indian politician from Bharatiya Janata Party currently serving as the Deputy Chief Minister of Rajasthan alongside Prem Chand Bairwa in the ministry of Bhajan Lal Sharma from 2023 December.

Rising from Minister for Forests and Agriculture to Austrian chancellor in 1932, this leader cemented dictatorial rule via a 1934 constitution before being killed in a Nazi-backed coup attempt — who was he?
Engelbert Dollfuss (alternatively Dollfu; 4 October 1892 - 25 July 1934) was an Austrian politician and dictator who served as chancellor of Austria between 1932 and 1934.

A former close aide to Chancellor Gerhard Schröder, this Social Democratic politician served twice as Germany's foreign minister and as vice-chancellor before becoming the country's president in 2017 — who is he?
Frank-Walter Steinmeier (born 5 January 1956) is a German politician who has served as President of Germany since 2017.
In 2022 this politician became the first woman to serve as Italy's prime minister; she has led the right-wing Brothers of Italy party since 2014 — who is she?
Giorgia Meloni (born 15 January 1977) is an Italian politician who has served as Prime Minister of Italy since October 2022.
This ancient Babylonian king conquered the rival city-states of Larsa, Eshnunna, and Mari during his reign in the 18th century BC, succeeding his father who abdicated due to poor health — who is he?
Hammurabi (c. 1810 BC - c. 1750 BC), also spelled Hammurapi, was the sixth Amorite king of Babylon, reigning from c. 1792 to c. 1750 BC.
This political system, in which members of a society hold a share of power and can hold their representatives accountable, stands in contrast to oligarchic and monarchic rule — what is it called?
History of democracy is a political system, or a system of decision-making within an institution, organization, or state, in which members have a share of power.
Which daughter of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra faced sacrifice at Aulis after her father offended Artemis, and in some myths escapes to reunite later with her brother Orestes?
Iphigenia (Ancient) was a daughter of King Agamemnon and Queen Clytemnestra, and thus a princess of Mycenae.
A former Salesian priest who taught liberation theology, this Haitian leader served as president multiple times — and spent years in exile after being toppled by coups. Who is he?

Jean-Bertrand Aristide (French; born 15 July 1953) is a Haitian former Salesian priest and politician who served as president of Haiti in 1991, from 1993 to 1994, from 1994 to 1996, and from 2001 to 2004.
Born into a poor Georgian family in Gori, this leader codified his party's official creed as Marxism–Leninism and ruled the Soviet Union as a dictator until his 1953 death — who was he?
Joseph Stalin was Leader of the Soviet Union from 1924 to 1953.
This California Republican served as the 55th Speaker of the House from January to October 2023, before resigning. He had represented California districts from 2007 onward. Who is he?
Kevin McCarthy (born January 26, 1965) is an American politician who served as the 55th speaker of the United States House of Representatives from January to October 2023.
This Polish president died in a 2010 plane crash near Smolensk, having previously served as mayor of Warsaw and, before that, headed the country's Supreme Audit Office — who was he?
Lech Kaczyński (18 June 1949 - 10 April 2010) was a Polish politician who served as the 4th president of Poland from 2005 to 2010, when he died in the Smolensk air disaster.
Born in Prague and fleeing a communist coup at age eleven, this Wellesley graduate climbed all the way to become the first woman to serve as U.S. Secretary of State — who was she?

Madeleine Albright (born Marie Jana Krbelov; May 15, 1937 - March 23, 2022) was an American diplomat and political scientist who served as the 64th United States secretary of state under President Bill Clinton from 1997 to 2001.
Born in 1946, which longtime Kurdistan Democratic Party leader governed as President of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq for over a decade starting in 2005?

Masoud Barzani (born 16 August 1946) is a Kurdish politician who has been leader of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) since 1979, and was President of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq from 2005 to 2017.
A rear admiral who fought at the Strait of Otranto, this Hungarian statesman governed his landlocked kingdom as regent from 1920 through most of World War II — an admiral without a sea. Who was he?

Miklós Horthy (18 June 1868 - 9 February 1957) was a Hungarian admiral and statesman who was the regent of the Kingdom of Hungary during the interwar period and most of World War II, from 1 March 1920 to 15 October 1944.
Founded in 1939, this conservative Mexican political organization ended 71 years of continuous rule by a rival group when its candidate won the 2000 presidential election — which organization is it?

National Action Party (Mexico) is a conservative political party in Mexico founded in 1939. The National Action Party (Spanish: Partido Acción Nacional, PAN) is a conservative political party in Mexico founded in 1939.
This KGB bureau chief in London spied for British intelligence from 1974 until his dramatic 1985 exfiltration, after which Moscow sentenced him to death in absentia — who is he?
Oleg Gordievsky (assumed name: Anton Kelsen; 10 October 1938 - 4 March 2025) was a colonel of the KGB who became KGB resident-designate (rezident) and bureau chief in London and a British spy.

Also called Whit Sunday, this Christian holiday falls on the 49th day after Easter and commemorates the Holy Spirit descending on the apostles in Jerusalem, marking what's called the church's 'birthday' - name it?
Pentecost (also called Whit Sunday, Whitsunday or Whitsun) is a Christian holiday that takes place on the 49th day (50th day when inclusive counting is used) after Easter.

This Greek king of the Hellenistic era was among ancient Rome's fiercest early opponents, and his costly victories over the Romans inspired a phrase still used today for a win that costs too much — who was he?
Pyrrhus of Epirus (Ancient; 319/318-272 BC) was a Greek king and statesman of the Hellenistic period.

This Slovak politician has served as prime minister across four separate terms since 2006, making him his country's longest-serving head of government, after founding a left-wing party in 1999 — who is he?
Prince Albert Victor, Duke of Clarence and Avondale
Robert Fico (born 15 September 1964) is a Slovak politician and lawyer, who has served as the prime minister of Slovakia since 2023.

Named after a 1930s guerrilla leader who resisted U.S. occupation, this socialist Nicaraguan political party overthrew dictator Anastasio Somoza Debayle in the 1979 revolution, ending decades of his family's rule — what is it?

Sandinista National Liberation Front is a socialist political party in Nicaragua. The Sandinista National Liberation Front (Spanish: Frente Sandinista de Liberación Nacional, FSLN) is a socialist political party in Nicaragua.

Fighting for Finland against the Soviet Union in the brutal Winter War, this sniper is believed to have killed more than 500 enemy soldiers, making him the deadliest sniper in recorded history — who was he?

Simo Häyhä (17 December 1905 - 1 April 2002), often referred to by his nickname The White Death, was a Finnish military sniper during the Winter War between Finland and the Soviet Union in World War II.
In Greek myth, this figure was punished in the underworld, made to stand in a pool beneath a fruit tree, with food and water eternally receding whenever he tried to eat or drink. Who was he?

Tantalus (Ancient Greek: Tantalos), also called Atys, was a Greek mythological figure, most famous for his punishment in Tartarus: he was made to stand in a pool of water beneath a fruit tree, with the fruit and water always receding whenever he tried to eat or drink.
With no central authority and worship held at autonomous centros or terreiros, this Brazilian faith's followers venerate spirit guides known as pretos velhos and caboclos — what religion is this?
Umbanda (Portuguese) is a religion that emerged in Brazil during the 1920s.

Having studied Japanese before joining his country's foreign ministry, this Chinese diplomat now directs the Communist Party's foreign affairs commission office while also serving as Minister of Foreign Affairs — who is he?

Wang Yi (pinyin: Wng Y; born 19 October 1953) is a Chinese diplomat and politician who is the director of the Central Committee Foreign Affairs Commission Office of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and Minister of Foreign Affairs.
This Korean admiral is remembered for winning every one of at least 23 naval battles he fought against the Japanese navy during a 16th-century war — who was he?
Yi Sun-sin (Korean; April 28, 1545 - December 16, 1598) was a Korean admiral and military general known for his victories against the Japanese navy during the Imjin War in the Joseon period.
The 34th and last sultan to truly control the fracturing Ottoman Empire, he lost Egypt, Cyprus, and Bulgaria yet won a war against Greece in 1897 — who was he?
Abdul Hamid II: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1876 to 1909.
Once a rebel commander known by the nom de guerre Abu Mohammad al-Julani, he led the offensives that toppled the Assad regime and became president of Syria in 2025 — who is he?
Ahmed al-Sharaa: President of Syria since 2025. Al-Sharaa joined al-Qaeda in Iraq shortly before the 2003 invasion of Iraq and fought for three years in the Iraqi insurgency.
He founded the Anti-Corruption Foundation in 2011 and famously branded Russia's ruling party a "party of crooks and thieves" — which Sakharov Prize-winning prisoner of conscience?
Alexei Navalny: Russian opposition leader and activist (1976–2024)
Appointed by President Joko Widodo in November 2021, this retired general became Indonesia's top military commander after rocketing from one-star to four-star rank in just five years — who is he?
An Israeli general turned politician, he helped create the army's Unit 101, fought in conflicts from 1948 through the Six-Day War, and later served as prime minister from 2001 — who?
Ariel Sharon: Prime Minister of Israel from 2001 to 2006.
Formed in 1428 as an alliance of three Nahua city-states ruling the Valley of Mexico, this civilization fell to Hernán Cortés and his allies in 1521 — what was it?
Aztec Empire: Alliance of three Nahua city states in Mexico (1428–1521). Its people and civil society are historiographically referred to as the Aztecs or the Culhua-Mexica.

This Ottoman sultan ruled from 1481 to 1512, welcomed Sephardi Jews expelled from Spain following the 1492 Alhambra Decree, and eventually abdicated his throne to his son, Selim I. Which sultan is this?
Bayezid II: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1481 to 1512. Bayezid; 3 December 1447/1448 – 26 May 1512) was the sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1481 to 1512.
Believed to have been an NKVD informant, he ran communist Poland from 1948 to 1956, stacking the offices of president, prime minister and party general secretary — who was he?
He lost his father in a 1947 plane crash at just nine months old and became heir to the throne at age four; reigning since 1973, he is the longest-serving monarch in his nation's history. Who is he?
Carl XVI Gustaf: King of Sweden since 1973.
An Argentine medical student so appalled by the poverty he saw touring South America that he joined a revolution, his stylized face became a global symbol of rebellion — who is he?
Serving from 2005 to 2009, this diplomat became the first female African-American U.S. secretary of state, having earlier been the first woman to serve as national security advisor — who is she?
Condoleezza Rice: American diplomat and political scientist (born 1954)
Taking office at age 35, this president became his country's youngest elected leader after Ecuador's National Assembly was dissolved via a constitutional mechanism in 2023 — who is he?
Daniel Noboa: President of Ecuador since 2023. Before his political career, Noboa served in several positions at Noboa Corporation, an exporting business founded by his grandfather.
A former socialist and economist who chairs the New Development Bank, she remains the only woman to hold Brazil's presidency, serving until her 2016 impeachment — who is she?
Dilma Rousseff: President of Brazil from 2011 to 2016.
Alongside Tenzing Norgay, this New Zealand mountaineer became one of the first two people confirmed to reach the top of Mount Everest, on 29 May 1953 — who is he?

Rising from a royal concubine to regent of the Qing dynasty, this Manchu noblewoman effectively ruled China from 1861 until her death in 1908, at one point installing her own nephew on the throne — who was she?
Empress Dowager Cixi: Regent of China from 1861 to 1908. Cixi was selected as a concubine of the Xianfeng Emperor in her adolescence and gave birth to his son, Zaichun, in 1856.
Aided by his interpreter La Malinche and thousands of Tlaxcaltec allies, Hernán Cortés ended the Aztec civilization with this 1521 siege — what's the event called?
Fall of Tenochtitlan: 1521 conquest of the Aztec capital by the Spanish Empire and rival indigenous tribes.
Officially the 'Spanish State,' this dictatorship with fascist features grew out of the Nationalist side of a civil war and ruled the whole country until its strongman's death in 1975. What was it?
Francoist Spain: Period of Spanish history (1936–1975)
Before running California, which leader co-founded the PlumpJack winery in Oakville with billionaire heir Gordon Getty as his backer?
Gavin Newsom: Governor of California since 2019.

Appearing in the Hebrew Bible, New Testament, and Quran as either individuals, tribes, or lands, this apocalyptic pairing is prophesied to be defeated near the 'end of days,' ushering in the Messianic Age — who or what are they?
Gog and Magog: Pair of individuals, peoples, or lands in the Bible and the Quran.
Born in what's now southern Spain, this Roman emperor of the Nerva–Antonine dynasty married Trajan's grandniece before succeeding him in 117 — who?

Often depicted holding twin torches and accompanied by dogs, this Greek goddess of crossroads, night, and magic first appears in Hesiod's 'Theogony' and was worshipped in Athens as a protector of the household — who is she?
Hecate: Greek goddess of magic and transitions. The earliest evidence for Hecate's cult comes from Selinunte, in Sicily.
Also known as Brahmanism, this ancient belief system of Indo-Aryan peoples in Punjab and the western Ganges plain (c. 1500-500 BCE) gave rise to today's Hinduism — what was it called?
Historical Vedic religion: 1500–500 BC Indo-Aryan religious practices of northwest India.
This French historian of Russian history served as Perpetual Secretary of the Académie Française from 1999 until her death in 2023 — who is she?
Hélène Carrère d'Encausse: French historian (1929–2023). Carrère d'Encausse was a member of the European Parliament between 1994 and 1999, representing the Gaullist-conservative party RPR.
Co-owner of Macy's department store and briefly a U.S. congressman, this businessman died aboard the Titanic after his wife refused to leave the ship without him — who is he?
Isidor Straus: American politician, businessman, and Titanic sinking victim (1845–1912)
A protégé of Andrew Jackson, this expansionist 11th president brought Texas into the Union and pushed American territory all the way to the Pacific in a single four-year term — who was he?
James K. Polk: President of the United States from 1845 to 1849.

In 1127 the Jurchen-led Jin army sacked the Northern Song capital and carted off two emperors at once — a captured ruler and his retired father — in a catastrophe the Chinese still call a 'Humiliation.' Which episode was it?
Jingkang incident: Part of the Jin–Song wars (1127)
Leader of the ABAKO party and a champion of independence from Belgium, he forged an unlikely coalition with Lumumba to become his country's first president in 1960 — who was this Congolese statesman?
Joseph Kasa-Vubu: 1st President of the Republic of the Congo.
This warrior united the Hawaiian Islands under a single crown and was later honored with a statue in Washington's National Statuary Hall — who was he?
Kamehameha I: King of Hawaii from 1795 to 1819.

Named by the prophet Mani as one of the four great powers of the 3rd century — alongside Persia, Rome, and China — this African realm was centered on a city in what's now Eritrea and northern Ethiopia. What was it?
Kingdom of Aksum: Polity in Africa and Arabia before 960.
This Guinean general seized power in a 1984 coup and then ruled the West African nation as its second president until his death in 2008 — who was he?
Lansana Conté: President of Guinea from 1984 to 2008.

The first woman to serve as chief of naval operations and the first ROTC graduate to hold the post, she also became the first woman on the Joint Chiefs of Staff before being relieved in 2025 — who is she?
Sparked by King Antiochus IV's ban on Jewish religious practices in 168 BCE, this uprising against Seleucid rule eventually won the rebels independence in Judea — which historic rebellion?

Maccabean Revolt: Jewish rebellion against the Seleucids. The rebels as a whole would come to be known as the Maccabees, and their actions would be chronicled later in the books of 1 Maccabees and 2 Maccabees.
Born and raised in Miami, this Republican rose from Florida House speaker to U.S. senator before becoming America's 72nd secretary of state in 2025 — who is he?
Marco Rubio: American politician and diplomat (born 1971)
This US Army general led the 82nd Airborne in Sicily, Italy and Normandy, later commanded a corps at the Battle of the Bulge, and went on to be Supreme Allied Commander Europe — who was he?
Matthew Ridgway: United States Army general (1895–1993)
Holding the title 2nd Marquis of Estella, this Spanish military officer ruled as dictator-prime minister from 1923 to 1930 during the twilight of the Bourbon Restoration — who is he?
Miguel Primo de Rivera: Prime Minister of Spain from 1923 to 1930. The coup enjoyed the acquiescence of the monarch, and Primo de Rivera was ensuingly tasked to form a government.

Across Hinduism, Jainism, Buddhism and Sikhism, this term names liberation from the cycle of death and rebirth — in Hindu tradition the highest of life's four aims, beside dharma, artha and kama. What is it?
Moksha: Spiritual liberation in Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism. In its epistemological and psychological senses, moksha requires self-realization, self-actualization, and self-knowledge.
Nephew of a far more famous emperor, he was first elected President of France in 1848, then crowned emperor in 1852, ushering in rapid industrialization — who was he?
Napoleon III: Emperor of the French from 1852 to 1870.
Commanded by God to build an ark ahead of a great flood, this biblical patriarch later became the first person to cultivate a vineyard — who is he?
Noah: Biblical prophet known for building an ark.
This legendary Thracian musician could charm even stones with his lyre, sailed with Jason in search of the Golden Fleece, and journeyed into the underworld to reclaim his dead wife — who is he?
Orpheus: Legendary musician, poet, and prophet in Greek mythology.
This Finnish Green League politician served as Foreign Minister from 2019 to 2023 and became the first openly gay candidate to run for his country's presidency — who is he?
Born in the late 19th century and often hurled as an insult, this contested political stance pits the so-called 'common people' against a perceived elite — what is it?
Populism: Political ideology emphasising the "common people"
Serving as Ecuador's president from 2007 to 2017, this democratic socialist economist has lived in Belgium since leaving office — who is he?
Rafael Correa: President of Ecuador from 2007 to 2017. Correa won the presidency in the 2006 general election on a platform criticizing the established political elites.
Which Titan tricked her husband into swallowing a rock instead of their infant son, having already borne five other future Olympian gods?
Rhea (mythology): Ancient Greek goddess and mother of the gods.
He founded Electronic Data Systems and never carried a single state, yet his 1992 and 1996 runs were among the strongest third-party showings in U.S. history — which Texan businessman was it?
Ross Perot: American businessman and politician (1930–2019)
Named for a 1930s guerrilla leader who resisted US occupation, this Nicaraguan socialist party toppled the Somoza dynasty in 1979 and governed through the 1980s — which party?
Sandinista National Liberation Front: Nicaraguan socialist political party founded in 1961.
This Russian nihilist preached revolution "by any means necessary" and fled the country in 1869 after taking part in the murder of a former comrade who'd dared to disagree with him — who was he?
Ending on the Fourth of July, 1863, this brutal Mississippi River campaign saw Grant trap Pemberton's Confederates in a fortress city — completing the Anaconda Plan's grip on the river. What was it?
Siege of Vicksburg: Battle of the American Civil War.
Son of a Greek Catholic priest in Galicia, he led a radical faction of Ukrainian nationalists and orchestrated the 1934 assassination of a Polish interior minister — who was he?
Born in Doha in 1980, this man only became heir after an older brother renounced the throne — and he's reigned over his Gulf nation since 2013. Who is he?
Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani: Emir of Qatar since 2013.
Brother of King Henry VIII's third wife, this nobleman married the king's widow Catherine Parr in 1547 while sparring with his own brother for influence over the young King Edward VI — who was he?
Thomas Seymour, 1st Baron Seymour of Sudeley
Thomas Seymour, 1st Baron Seymour of Sudeley: English nobleman (1508–1548)
Thomas Seymour, 1st Baron Seymour of Sudeley
The first Asian to lead the United Nations, this Burmese diplomat served a record ten years and one month as Secretary-General starting in 1961 — who was he?
U Thant: UN Secretary-General from 1961 to 1971.

Spanning roughly 800 to 1050 CE, this era of Norse raiding, trading, and settlement saw Scandinavians reach as far as Newfoundland, becoming the first Europeans known to set foot in North America. What period was this?
Viking Age: Period of European history (about 800–1050)

The first conflict of the Napoleonic Wars, this 1805–1806 struggle pitted Napoleon's France against an alliance of Britain, Austria, Russia, Naples, Sicily, and Sweden, and included the Battle of Trafalgar — which conflict?
War of the Third Coalition: 1805–1806 conflict during the Napoleonic Wars. The Royal Navy, however, assured its naval dominance at the Battle of Trafalgar in October 1805.
The longest-serving member of any democratic German parliament, this CDU politician served as president of the Bundestag from 2017 to 2021 — who was he?

Regarded as the fourth person to accept Islam, this former slave became the adopted son of the Prophet Muhammad and later commanded early Muslim military expeditions, including a final raid on Byzantine-held Bosra in 629 CE — who was he?
Zayd ibn Haritha al-Kalbi: Companion and adopted son of the Islamic prophet Muhammad.
Which of these people was born first?
Qian Xuesen (born 1911) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Qian Xuesen (born 1911) is the earliest of the four. Qian received his undergraduate education in mechanical engineering at National Chiao Tung University in Shanghai in 1934.
Which one below was established earliest?
Python (programming language) (founded 1991) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the astronomer from these four.
Fritz Zwicky is an astronomer. Fritz Zwicky (German: [ˈtsvɪki]; February 14, 1898 – February 8, 1974) was a Swiss astronomer.
Which of these four is a mathematician?
Hilary Putnam is a mathematician. Outside philosophy, Putnam contributed to mathematics and computer science.
What is the atomic number of Antimony?
Antimony is a chemical element with the symbol Sb (from Latin stibium) and atomic number 51.
What is the atomic number of Chromium?
Chromium is a chemical element; it has symbol Cr and atomic number 24.
In what year was Nikola Tesla born?
Nikola Tesla (10 July 1856 – 7 January 1943) was a Serbian-American engineer, futurist, and inventor.
In what year was Möbius strip discovered?
Möbius strip: In mathematics, a Möbius strip, Möbius band, or Möbius loop is a surface that can be formed by attaching the ends of a strip of paper together with a half-twist.
R (programming language): Robert Gentleman. R is a programming language for statistical computing and data visualization.
Prunus domestica: People's Republic of China. Prunus domestica is a species of flowering plant in the family Rosaceae.
Which country is McDonnell Douglas F-15E Strike Eagle from?

McDonnell Douglas F-15E Strike Eagle: United States. The McDonnell Douglas (now Boeing) F-15E Strike Eagle is an American all-weather multirole strike fighter derived from the McDonnell Douglas F-15 Eagle.
Who is credited with discovering Nihonium?
Nihonium: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research. Nihonium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Nh and atomic number 113.
Who is credited with discovering Mass–energy equivalence?
Mass–energy equivalence: Albert Einstein. In physics, mass–energy equivalence is the relationship between mass and energy in a system's rest frame.
Who is credited with discovering Plesiosaurus?
Plesiosaurus: Mary Anning. It is known by nearly complete skeletons from the Lias of England.
First nominated by Ronald Reagan in 1987 and reappointed every four years until 2006, this economist ran the Federal Reserve for its second-longest tenure ever — who is he?
Alan Greenspan (born March 6, 1926) is an American economist who served as the 13th chairman of the Federal Reserve from 1987 to 2006.
This English number theorist became a mathematical legend by proving Fermat's Last Theorem, earning the 2016 Abel Prize and a knighthood. Who is he?
Andrew Wiles (born 11 April 1953) is an English mathematician and a Royal Society Research Professor at the University of Oxford, specialising in number theory.

A German former computer repair technician, this man received international attention after murdering and cannibalizing a voluntary victim he had found over the Internet in March 2001, and was ultimately convicted of murder in a 2006 retrial — who is he?

Armin Meiwes (born 1 December 1961) is a German former computer repair technician who received international attention for murdering and cannibalising Bernd Brandes, whom he had found via the Internet as a voluntary victim, in March 2001.
The second-largest living rodents after capybaras, these large semiaquatic mammals of the Northern Hemisphere have webbed back feet, hand-like front paws, and flat, scaly tails — name the animal?
Beaver (genus Castor) are large semiaquatic rodents of the Northern Hemisphere.

Believed to descend from hounds kept at a Belgian abbey and used by police worldwide to track escaped prisoners, this scent hound can discern a person's trail days after they've passed — name this dog breed?
Bloodhound is a large scent hound, originally bred for hunting deer, wild boar, rabbits, and since the Middle Ages, for tracking people.
This condition results from inflamed, fluid-filled sacs that cushion friction points between bones, tendons, and muscles, commonly striking the shoulder, elbow, hip, or knee — what is it?
Bursitis is the inflammation of one or more bursae in the body.
This large, stocky black corvid fills a niche across Eurasia comparable to a similar bird found in North America, but is bigger and huskier than its transatlantic counterpart — what species is it?
Carrion crow (Corvus corone) is a passerine bird of the family Corvidae, native to western Europe and the eastern Palearctic.
Besides identifying the laws of elastic collision, this Dutch polymath studied Saturn's rings and improved the design of the telescope — who is he?
Christiaan Huygens (14 April 1629 - 8 July 1695) was a Dutch mathematician, physicist, engineer, astronomer, and inventor who is regarded as a key figure in the Scientific Revolution.
This activity involves designing algorithms and writing code in high-level languages so a machine can follow step-by-step instructions to perform tasks. What is it?
Computer programming is the composition of sequences of instructions, called programs, that computers can follow to perform tasks.
This Zambian-born economist turned four of her five books into New York Times bestsellers, including a provocative argument that foreign aid actually holds Africa back — who is she?
Dambisa Moyo, Baroness Moyo (born 2 February 1969) is a Zambian-born economist and author, known for her analysis of macroeconomics and global affairs.
Made from a fermented batter of ground black gram and rice, this thin South Indian bread is traditionally served with chutney and sambar — what is it?

Dosa (food) (in Indian English) or thosai (in Malaysian English and Singapore English) is a thin, savoury batter bread in South Indian cuisine made from a fermented batter of ground black gram and rice.

These ductless glands throughout the body secrete their products directly into the bloodstream rather than through a duct — together with the pineal, pituitary, thyroid, and others, what are they called?
Endocrine gland is a network of glands and organs located throughout the body.
This Chinese-born American computer scientist built ImageNet, the dataset that supercharged computer vision in the 2010s, and co-directs Stanford's Human-Centered AI institute — who is she?

Fei-Fei Li (pinyin: L Fifi; born July 3, 1976) is a Chinese-born American computer scientist best known for establishing ImageNet, the dataset that enabled rapid advances in computer vision in the 2010s.

Found from the tropics to subarctic regions and accounting for about 88% of living amphibian species, this tailless, semiaquatic creature has a name that informally splits into 'toad' for the warty ones — what is it?
Frog is any member of a diverse and largely semiaquatic group of short-bodied, tailless amphibian vertebrates composing the order Anura (coming from the Ancient Greek, literally 'without tail').
One of the most widely distributed eagles in the Northern Hemisphere, this raptor is dark brown with lighter plumage on its nape and white markings on immature birds — which bird of prey?
Golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos) is a bird of prey living in the Northern Hemisphere.

This now-outdated astronomical model placed the Sun rather than the Earth at the center of the universe, eventually replacing the geocentric view before itself being superseded by relativity — what model is it?
Heliocentrism (also known as the heliocentric model) is a superseded astronomical model that placed the Sun at the center of the universe, with the Earth and the planets in its orbit.

Also called prussic acid, this highly toxic and flammable liquid boils just above room temperature at 25.6 degrees Celsius. It is produced industrially as a precursor to many chemical compounds, particularly potassium cyanide and adiponitrile. What is it?
Hydrogen cyanide (also called prussic acid) is a chemical compound with the formula HCN and structural formula HCN.
Founder of Romania's Social Democratic Party, this engineer served two separate stints as president after playing a leading role in the 1989 revolution that toppled Ceaușescu — who is he?

Ion Iliescu (3 March 1930 - 5 August 2025) was a Romanian politician and engineer who served as the first and third President of Romania since the country's transition to democracy, from 1990 to 1996 and 2000 to 2004.
Originally trained as a mathematician, this English economist built the foundation for an entire school of macroeconomic thought that bears his name — who is he?

John Maynard Keynes (KAYNZ; 5 June 1883 - 21 April 1946), was an English economist whose writings are considered the basis for the school of thought known as Keynesian economics, as well as its various offshoots.
When the natural curve of the thoracic spine exceeds about 45 degrees, doctors give this excessive rounding of the upper back a name rooted in the Greek word for 'hump' — what is it?
Kyphosis (from Greek (kyphos) 'hump') is an abnormally excessive convex curvature of the spine as it occurs in the thoracic and sacral regions.
Serving as a somatosensory organ as well as a tool for eating and forming sounds, this pair of soft facial features is one of the most visible parts of the mouth — what are they?
Lip are a horizontal pair of soft appendages attached to the jaws and are the most visible part of the mouth of many animals, including humans.
Roughly 60% the diameter of Pluto and stained reddish-brown by tholins, this trans-Neptunian dwarf planet carries minor-planet number 136472 — what is it?
Makemake (minor-planet number 136472) is a dwarf planet orbiting the Sun in the Kuiper belt, a disc of icy bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune.
This genus of about 20 species in the Lamiaceae family readily hybridizes where different species' ranges overlap, and thrives best in wet, moist soils — what genus is it?
Mentha (from Greek mntha, Linear B mi-ta), is a genus of flowering plants in the mint family, Lamiaceae.

Native to Africa, Asia, and Oceania, with one invasive species now in the southern U.S., this reptile genus ranges from 20 centimeters long to over 3 meters in the Komodo dragon — name this group of lizards?
Monitor lizard are lizards in the genus Varanus, the only extant genus in the family Varanidae.

Discovered in 1898 alongside krypton and xenon, this colorless noble gas is famous for the distinctive bright-red glow it emits, which led to its immediate identification as a new element — what gas, symbol Ne, is it?
Neon is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ne and the atomic number 10.

This branch of medicine focuses on the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of cancer, a disease first documented in Egypt as early as 3000 BCE in the Edwin Smith papyrus — what is this medical specialty called?
Oncology is a branch of medicine that deals with the study, treatment, diagnosis, and prevention of cancer.
Named after a 17th-century French mathematician and physicist, this SI unit of pressure is defined as one newton of force per square metre — name the unit?
Pascal (unit) (symbol: Pa) is the unit of pressure in the International System of Units (SI).
Ranging in color from clear to yellow, green, or even grey, this respiratory mucus is expelled through coughing and also goes by the name sputum — what is it?
Phlegm (Ancient) is mucus produced by the respiratory system, excluding that produced by the throat and nose passages.
Ranging from linear chains to heavily branched polymers, these carbohydrate compounds — like starch, glycogen, and chitin — consist of many simple sugar units linked together. What are they called?
Polysaccharide (from Ancient Greek (pols) 'many, much' and (skkhar) 'sugar') are "compounds consisting of a large number of monosaccharides linked glycosidically".
Nesting in burrows or rock crevices on coastal cliffs, this black-and-white seabird can dive underwater to feed and beats its short wings up to 400 times per minute in flight — what bird is it?
Puffin are any of three species of small alcids (auks) in the bird genus Fratercula.
Which large Southern African dog breed, whose standard was drafted in 1922 in what's now Zimbabwe, descends from ridged hunting dogs of the Khoikhoi crossed with European breeds used to bay lions?
Rhodesian Ridgeback is a large dog breed originally bred in Southern Africa.
Once placed in its own plant family before molecular studies folded it into Dracaena, this African and Asian succulent genus includes the plant nicknamed 'devil's tongue' — which genus?

Sansevieria is a historically recognized genus of flowering plants, native to Africa, notably Madagascar, and southern Asia, now included in the genus Dracaena on the basis of molecular phylogenetic studies.
Named for its enormous shoe-shaped bill, this grey wading bird of East African swamps was once filed with storks but now sits beside pelicans — and its closest kin is the hamerkop — what is it?
Shoebill (Balaeniceps rex), also known as the whale-headed stork, whalebill, and shoe-billed stork, is a large long-legged wading bird.

This class of moisture-loving hexapods — the largest lineage of six-legged creatures excluded from the insect group — indirectly aids decomposition by breaking down organic matter and shaping soil microbial life. What are they?
Springtail (class Collembola) form the largest of the three lineages of modern hexapods that are no longer considered insects, the others being Protura and Diplura.
Serving as prime minister seven separate times before becoming president from 1993 to 2000, this Turkish statesman led two different political parties across his long career — who was he?
Süleyman Demirel (1 November 1924 - 17 June 2015) was a Turkish politician, engineer, and statesman who served as the president of Turkey from 1993 to 2000.
This herb is also called common thyme or garden thyme and belongs to the mint family, Lamiaceae — which species is it?
Thymus vulgaris (common thyme, German thyme, garden thyme or just thyme) is a species of flowering plant in the mint family, Lamiaceae.
This break in the skin or mucous membrane involves tissue breakdown severe enough to expose the dermis or fat beneath, and often becomes infected with pus — what condition is it?
Ulcer (dermatology) is a sore on the skin or a mucous membrane, accompanied by the disintegration of tissue.
This unit of time, equal to seven days, serves as the standard calendrical period between a day and a month in most of the world. What is it?
Week (in the Western and international context) is a unit of time equal to seven days.
Also known as the empirical guideline, this statistical shorthand describes the percentage of values within one, two, and three standard deviations of the mean in a normal distribution — which one?
Transmitted by the bite of an infected tsetse fly, this parasitic infection caused by Trypanosoma brucei is better known in humans as 'sleeping sickness' — what's its formal name?
African trypanosomiasis: Parasitic disease also known as sleeping sickness.
With more than 1,100 species including onions, garlic, leeks, and chives, this is the largest genus in the flowering plant family Amaryllidaceae — which genus?
Allium: Genus of flowering plants. The flowers form an umbel at the top of a leafless stalk.
This Russian physicist miraculously survived a 1978 accident in which a high-energy proton beam from a particle accelerator passed directly through his skull — who is he?
Anatoli Bugorski: Soviet and Russian scientist (born 1942)
Known by common names like greenfly and blackfly, these small sap-sucking insects reproduce via live-born nymphs without males, a trick called telescoping generations — what are they?
Aphid: Superfamily of insects. The group includes the fluffy white woolly aphids.
Originally conceived as the average Earth-Sun distance before its 2012 redefinition, this measure equals about 499 light-seconds and underpins the definition of the parsec — what is it called?
Astronomical unit: Mean distance between Earth and the Sun.
The most common type of skin cancer, this slow-growing tumor is sometimes called a 'rodent ulcer' and rarely spreads beyond its original site — what is it?
Basal-cell carcinoma: Most common type of skin cancer. Basal-cell carcinoma (BCC), also known as basal-cell cancer, basalioma, or rodent ulcer, is the most common type of skin cancer.
Coined by Károly Ereky in 1919, this multidisciplinary field harnesses bacteria, yeast, and plants — often via genetic engineering — to create products and services. What field?
Biotechnology: Use of living systems and organisms to develop or make useful products.
Certified in Canada in 1998, this large-cabin business jet shares its fuselage cross-section with the Challenger 600 and first flew in 1996 — which jet is it?
Bombardier Global Express: Large cabin business jet. The Bombardier Global Express is a large cabin, long-range business jet designed and manufactured by Bombardier Aviation.

Comprising over 250 species that form small colonies of as few as 50 individuals around a single queen, these fuzzy insects were introduced to New Zealand and Tasmania and can sting repeatedly without dying — which insect is it?
Bumblebee: Genus of insect. A bumblebee (or bumble bee, bumble-bee, or humble-bee) is any of over 250 species in the genus Bombus, part of Apidae, one of the bee families.
Designated Alpha Carinae and located some 310 light-years away, this bright giant is the second-brightest star in the night sky, outshone only by Sirius — which star?
Canopus: Brightest star in the constellation of Carina.
A first-generation cephalosporin and β-lactam, this antibiotic can be taken by mouth and treats ear, bone, skin and urinary infections by disrupting bacterial cell-wall growth — what is it?
Cefalexin: Beta-lactam antibiotic. Cefalexin, also spelled cephalexin, is an antibiotic that can treat a number of bacterial infections.

First recorded in the 3rd-to-5th-century manuscript Sunzi Suanjing, this number-theory result lets you deduce what's left over after dividing by a product of coprime numbers, just from the leftovers after dividing by each one — which principle?
Chinese remainder theorem: About simultaneous modular congruences.
Native to Indonesia's Maluku Islands, these aromatic flower buds flavor your food but also turn up in toothpaste and soaps — what spice are they?
Clove: Spice made from flower buds.
Often defined as the transmission of information, this concept is famously modeled as a source encoding a message, sending it through a channel, and a receiver decoding it — what is it?
Communication: Transmission of information. Models of communication are simplified overviews of its main components and their interactions.
A group of these black birds is famously called a 'murder,' and their larger cousins are known as ravens — what bird is this?
Crow: Index of animals with the same common name.
The second jet fighter to enter RAF service and the first powered by a single jet engine, this twin-boom aircraft flew with the Halford Goblin turbojet — which aircraft?

De Havilland Vampire: Fighter aircraft; first single-engine jet in RAF service. The de Havilland DH100 Vampire is a British jet fighter developed and manufactured by the de Havilland Aircraft Company.
This category of mental health conditions involves an unconscious defense mechanism that fragments consciousness, memory, and identity to protect against traumatic stress — what is it called?
Dissociative disorder: Set of mental health conditions.
A pregnancy complication where the embryo attaches outside the uterus, classically presenting with abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. What is this condition?
Ectopic pregnancy: Female reproductive system health issue.
A sympathomimetic stimulant often used to keep blood pressure up during anesthesia, this drug has also been tried for asthma, narcolepsy, and obesity — what is it?

Ranging from Northern Europe through Siberia to the Himalayas, this medium-sized wild cat is one of only four living species in its genus and can be found at elevations up to 5,500 meters — what animal is this?
Eurasian lynx: Species of medium-sized cat native to Eurasia.

Named for the physicist who reportedly asked 'but where is everybody?' at Los Alamos in 1950, this puzzle questions why we've found no evidence of alien civilizations despite the odds favoring them — what's it called?
Fermi paradox: Discrepancy of the lack of evidence for alien life despite its apparent likelihood.
Alongside James Watson, this English scientist co-authored the 1953 Nature paper unveiling DNA's double helix and later coined the phrase 'central dogma' — who is he?
Francis Crick: English physicist and biologist (1916–2004)

Published by Einstein in 1916 as a refinement of Newton's law of gravitation, this geometric framework describes gravity as curved spacetime, summed up by Wheeler as 'space-time tells matter how to move; matter tells space-time how to curve'?
General relativity: Theory of gravitation as curved spacetime. The relation is specified by the Einstein field equations, a system of second-order partial differential equations.
Despite its common name, this Eurasian wolf-like canid is more closely related to wolves and coyotes than to its African namesakes — what animal is it?
Published in 1931 by an Austrian logician, these two results proved that any consistent axiom system for arithmetic will always contain true statements it cannot prove — what are they called?
Gödel's incompleteness theorems: Limitative results in mathematical logic.

This French mathematician reinvented what it means to find the area under a curve, publishing his sweeping new theory of integration in a 1902 dissertation titled "Integral, length, area." Who was he?
Strongly associated with human habitation and now the most widely distributed wild bird on Earth thanks to introductions across multiple continents, this small brown-and-black bird is which species?
House sparrow: Species of bird. The house sparrow (Passer domesticus) is a bird of the sparrow family Passeridae, found in most parts of the world.
Once down to just 94 individuals in Andalusia by 2002, largely due to a crash in its rabbit prey from myxomatosis, this medium-sized wild cat is endemic to a European peninsula — which species?
Iberian lynx: Species of mammal. The Iberian lynx (Lynx pardinus) is one of four extant species of Lynx, a genus of medium-sized wild cats.

He won the 1944 Nobel Prize for his resonance method of recording the magnetic properties of atomic nuclei, and was among the first Americans to work on the cavity magnetron behind radar and microwave ovens — which physicist?
This German craftsman's mechanical printing press — with its oil-based ink and adjustable metal type — sparked an information revolution that helped fuel the Renaissance and Reformation — who is he?
Johannes Gutenberg: German inventor and craftsman (c. 1393–1406 – 1468)

A NASA mathematician and human computer, she calculated the orbital mechanics critical to America's first crewed spaceflights and was among the first African-American women to work as a NASA scientist — who was she?
Native to the Mediterranean and used to season food as a bay leaf, this aromatic evergreen prominent in classical Greco-Roman culture can grow up to 20 metres tall — what is its scientific name?
Laurus nobilis: Species of flowering plant in the laurel family Lauraceae.
Soft, movable, and painless, this benign fatty-tissue growth most often shows up under the skin on the upper back, shoulders, or abdomen — what is it?
Lipoma: Benign tumor made of fat tissue.
This common, nonspecific medical sign involves lymph nodes becoming abnormally swollen or enlarged, with causes ranging from the common cold to cancer. What's the condition called?
Lymphadenopathy: Abnormal change in size of the lymph nodes.
This American cultural anthropologist's 1928 fieldwork, Coming of Age in Samoa, made her a household name for exploring adolescence and sexuality in Pacific societies — who is she?
Nicknamed a 'semi-lunar' cartilage for its half-moon shape, this crescent-shaped structure cushions joints like the knee, wrist, and jaw — what is it?
Meniscus (anatomy): Fibrocartilaginous part of a bone joint.
Known to NATO as 'Flogger,' this Soviet variable-sweep-wing fighter was the first in the country's air force to carry look-down/shoot-down radar, with over 5,000 built. Which aircraft?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-23: Soviet fighter-interceptor aircraft introduced in 1970.
Native to northern India, this fast-growing, drought-resistant tree is nicknamed the 'drumstick tree' for its seed pods and the 'horseradish tree' for its pungent roots — what is it?
Moringa oleifera: Species of flowering tree.
Made of two fused benzene rings, this pungent white crystalline compound is the main ingredient in traditional mothballs — what is it?
Naphthalene: Chemical compound. It is a white crystalline solid with a characteristic odor that is detectable at concentrations as low as 0.08 ppm.
Element 102 honors the inventor of dynamite, who endowed a famous set of prizes — fitting, since this synthetic metal can only be forged in particle accelerators. What is it?
Nobelium: Chemical element with atomic number 102 (No)
In this learning process, voluntary behaviors are shaped by their consequences — strengthened by reinforcement, weakened by punishment or extinction. What is it called?
Operant conditioning: Type of associative learning process for behavioral modification.
This B vitamin's name comes from the Greek for "from everywhere," since it turns up in nearly all foods, and animals need it to build coenzyme A — what is it?
Derived from the Latin for 'by a hundred,' this dimensionless number expresses a ratio as a fraction of 100 and is usually written with a % sign — what is it called?

Percentage: Number or ratio expressed as a fraction of 100. In mathematics, a percentage, percent, or per cent (from Latin per centum 'by a hundred') is a number or ratio expressed as a fraction of 100.
Their name blends the Greek for "plant" and "drifter": these self-feeding plankton photosynthesize in the sunlit surface waters of oceans and lakes — what are they?
Phytoplankton: Autotrophic members of the plankton ecosystem.
Native to Southeast Asia and tasting like a sweet grapefruit, this non-hybrid citrus is the largest of them all — in fact, an ancestor of both the grapefruit and the bitter orange — what is it?
Pomelo: Citrus fruit from Southeast Asia.
Created in the early 18th century, this dark pigment was the first modern synthetic color, made by oxidizing iron ferrocyanide salts — what is it?
Prussian blue: Synthetic pigment. Prussian blue (also known as Berlin blue, Brandenburg blue, Parisian and Paris blue) is a dark blue pigment produced by oxidation of ferrous ferrocyanide salts.
Element 88 reacts with nitrogen rather than oxygen in air, turning black, and once glowed in self-luminous paints despite being highly carcinogenic — which element is it?
Radium: Chemical element with atomic number 88 (Ra)
Curving around the chest, these bones protect the lungs and heart and, in snakes, support and protect the whole body — what are they called?
Rib: Long bone in vertebrates that protects vital respiratory and cardiovascular organs.
First identified in Wuhan in late 2019 and once provisionally called 2019-nCoV, this positive-sense RNA virus is the one that causes COVID-19 — what's its official name?
SARS-CoV-2: Virus that causes COVID-19. The virus previously had the provisional name 2019 novel coronavirus (2019-nCoV), and has also been called human coronavirus 2019 (HCoV-19 or hCoV-19).
Creator of a satirical comic strip about corporate cubicle life, this cartoonist also wrote the pandeistic novella 'God's Debris' — who is he?
Scott Adams: American cartoonist and author (1957–2026)
Named for a Swedish medical physicist, this SI unit measures the stochastic health risk of ionizing radiation, such as equivalent and effective dose — what unit is it?
Sievert: Derived SI unit of equivalent dose of ionizing radiation. One sievert equals 100 rem, which is an older, CGS radiation unit.
Also nicknamed 'sour dock,' this perennial herb native to Eurasia is often eaten as a tangy leaf vegetable in grassland habitats — which plant?
Sorrel: Flowering plant in the family Polygonaceae.
In this eye disorder, the two eyes fail to align properly on the same object, which can cause a lazy eye and lost depth perception if it persists through much of childhood. What condition is it?
Strabismus: Eyes not aligning when looking at something.
Commonly known as the pork tapeworm, this parasite completes its life cycle by cycling between human waste, pig feed, and undercooked pork — which species?
Taenia solium: Species of tapeworm. Taenia solium, the pork tapeworm, belongs to the cyclophyllid cestode family Taeniidae.
This Hungarian-American aerospace pioneer made crucial advances in supersonic and hypersonic airflow, and the agreed boundary of outer space — the "___ line" — bears his name. Who was he?
Theodore von Kármán: Hungarian-American mathematician, aerospace engineer and physicist (1881–1963)
Marketed as Topamax, this oral medication treats epilepsy and prevents migraines, though it can cause weight loss and kidney stones as side effects — what is it?
Topiramate: Medication used to treat epilepsy and migraine.
Spread by body lice, chiggers, or fleas depending on the strain, this group of bacterial diseases causes fever, headache, and rash, and is treated with the antibiotic doxycycline — what is it?
Typhus: Group of infectious diseases. Typhus, also known as typhus fever, is a group of infectious diseases that include epidemic typhus, scrub typhus, and murine typhus.
Posthumously awarded the Padma Vibhushan in 1972, this physicist and astronomer is regarded as the father of his country's space program — who is he?

Vikram Sarabhai: Indian physicist and astronomer. Often regarded as the "Father of Indian space program", Sarabhai was honored with Padma Bhushan in 1966 and the Padma Vibhushan (posthumously) in 1972.
Known also as the gnu, this African antelope comes in black and blue varieties whose lineages split roughly a million years ago — which animal?
Wildebeest: Genus of antelope. Wildebeest (WIL-di-beest;, VIL-,), also called gnu (NOO or, NEW), are antelopes of the genus Connochaetes and native to Eastern and Southern Africa.
Released from prison in June 2025, this Turkish politician resumed leading the nationalist Victory Party after previously serving as deputy leader of the MHP — who is he?
The symbol for radon is Rn. Radon is a chemical element; it has symbol Rn and atomic number 86.

Bernardo Bertolucci (born 1941) is the earliest of the four. Considered one of the greatest directors in the history of cinema, Bertolucci's work achieved international acclaim.

Which of these four is a comedian?
Gilda Radner is a comedian. Gilda Susan Radner (June 28, 1946 – May 20, 1989) was an American actress and comedian.
In what year was Michael Douglas born?
Michael Douglas: Michael Kirk Douglas (born September 25, 1944) is an American actor and film producer.
In what year was Steve Martin born?
Steve Martin: Stephen Glenn Martin (born August 14, 1945) is an American comedian, actor, writer, producer, and musician.
In what year was Joaquin Phoenix born?
Joaquin Phoenix: Joaquin Rafael Phoenix (whah-KEEN; né Bottom; October 28, 1974) is an American actor.
In what year was Bradley Cooper born?
Bradley Cooper: Bradley Charles Cooper (born January 5, 1975) is an American actor and filmmaker.
In what year was Sarah Shahi born?
